title: Pickthall and the 1934 translation
hook: two early English translations, both by Muslims, both still read

segments.voice: Yesterday, Arabic: the Qur'an as the Arabic itself, and a translation as its meanings. Your line was a translation is a meaning. What did a translation leave behind for you? Day three hundred twenty.

All year, when this path has quoted the Qur'an in English, you've heard one particular voice. Thee and thou. Lo! Verily. "But lo! with hardship goeth ease." That's Marmaduke Pickthall, an Englishman writing in 1930. Why him? Partly because his translation is old enough to be free for anyone to quote. But it's also one of two early English translations, both by Muslims, that people still read nearly a century later. Today: Pickthall, and the translation of 1934.
screen: `THEE, THOU, LO, VERILY.` → `AN ENGLISHMAN IN 1930.` → `TWO EARLY TRANSLATIONS.`

segments.voice: Pickthall was born in 1875, the son of an English country clergyman. He became a novelist, traveled in Syria, Palestine and Turkey, and grew to love the Muslim world he met there. In 1917, in London, he publicly declared himself a Muslim. Later he went to India and worked in the service of the Nizam of Hyderabad, who gave him leave to finish his translation. Before publishing, he took it to Cairo to go over it with scholars there. It appeared in 1930 as The Meaning of the Glorious Koran. His aim was to be almost literal, close to the Arabic's order, in the solemn English of the old Bible that his readers would recognize as scripture. That's why it can feel stiff, and why it can also feel like thunder. The second came from an Indian Muslim scholar who had served in the civil service in India, and began appearing in 1934. Its English is more flowing, set out in lines like poetry, and it carries thousands of explanatory notes, so reading it is like reading with a teacher at your shoulder. Later publishers revised some of those notes, so editions differ. For decades it was among the most widely printed English Qur'ans in the world. Two Muslims, two temperaments. One stays close to the Arabic's shape and lets you do the work. One opens the meaning out and explains as it goes. And that's the gift of reading more than one. Where they agree, you're probably close to the meaning. Where they differ, you've found a place where the Arabic holds more than one English sentence can carry.
screen: `AN ENGLISH NOVELIST BECOMES MUSLIM` · `ALMOST LITERAL, IN OLD ENGLISH` · `A SECOND VOICE, FROM 1934` · `WHERE THEY DIFFER, LOOK CLOSER`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one line in each. Start with Pickthall's line from Surah 94: "But lo! with hardship goeth ease." Say it slowly, twice. Feel its weight. After the bell, find the same verse in the 1934 translation, or any other you have, and read the two side by side. For now, stay with this one line. Where in your life is the hardship right now, and can you picture the ease already walking beside it? The bell holds the time.
Pickthall and the 1934 translation. Two early English renderings of the Qur'an's meanings, both by Muslims: one close and plain, one flowing and explained. Today's word.

Your line: two voices, one line. Today, when two people you trust describe the same thing differently, listen to both, and look for what each one sees that the other doesn't. Day three hundred twenty.

howItsDone: Many English-speaking Muslims read the Qur'an's meanings in more than one translation, often Pickthall's 1930 rendering alongside the 1934 translation and newer ones, usually printed beside the Arabic.
